name: PT HATTEN BALI Tbk

frontmatter.title: Hatten Bali: the only listed Indonesian winery, priced below the value of its stock
frontmatter.summary: Hatten Bali trades at 7.3x trailing earnings and 0.9x book after a de-rating from Rp270. The third-quarter 2026 filing, the only statement published since our first draft, shows the margin turn already happening; the audited year, annual report and half-year were available all along and this revision corrects that gap. Rating BUY, target Rp145.
thesis: The de-rating is overdone: 7.3x earnings and 6.0x EBITDA for a business still earning a low-teens return on equity and paying a rising dividend.

The margin trough was the first half: the nine months of 2026 carry IDR86.9bn of gross profit on IDR223.5bn of sales and the third quarter recovered on its own, so we no longer need an assumed back-end-loaded year.
Bali arrivals are down -1.1% in the first nine months of 2026, not collapsing, while retail and outside-Bali sales grew at double-digit rates on the same filing.
The balance sheet holds IDR24.7bn of investment property outside the operating business and bank debt was repaid to IDR51.2bn by 30 September 2026.
The controlling shareholder bought stock at the market in November 2026 above today's price - a small but unambiguous signal in a name with no research coverage.

catalysts.event: BPS Bali monthly foreign-arrival release for October 2026
FY2026 audited results: first full year on the new excise and raw-material cost base
FY2026 dividend decision and ex-date, against the house payout record
First-half 2027 filing: the test of whether the third-quarter 2026 margin held through a low season

blocks.text: Hatten Bali is the only wine producer listed in Indonesia and, on our numbers, priced for a business that has stopped earning. At Rp106 the shares trade on 7.3x FY2025 earnings, 6.0x EBITDA and 0.9x book, against a fifty-two week high of Rp270 [S0]. Our twelve-month target is Rp145, a total return of 40.0% including the Rp3.5 trailing dividend, and our rating is BUY.

This is a revision, and it corrects an evidence gap rather than reporting a change in the facts. The first draft was built on the first-quarter filing and the vendor pack's June balance sheet while the audited FY2025 accounts, the 2025 annual report and the second-quarter 2026 filing were already public [S10][S13][S12]; only the third-quarter statement is new since that draft [S11]. Naming that plainly matters, because the upgrade rests on numbers the first draft could have used. What the fuller evidence changes is threefold. Nine months of 2026 are now actual: net sales IDR223.5bn, gross profit IDR86.9bn and net profit IDR29.7bn, and the third quarter on its own grew faster than the first half [S11]. The balance sheet repaid bank debt to IDR51.2bn with cash of IDR3.7bn, leaving equity attributable to shareholders at IDR357.2bn against a market capitalisation below it [S11]. And the accounts carry IDR24.7bn of investment property - unused land bought in December 2025 - that produces no operating cash flow and was missing from our first valuation [S11].

The market is making a specific bet: that the fall in gross margin from the mid-forties in FY2024 to the high thirties now is permanent, and that a winery on an island whose foreign arrivals fell -1.1% in the first nine months of 2026 has no growth left [S10][S5]. Half of that is right. The cost step-up is real - raw materials used in production ran at IDR20.8bn in the first quarter against less than half of that a year earlier - and we hold gross margin near 39.1% through the forecast rather than assume it back at the FY2024 level [S2]. But the first half was the trough, not the trend: the nine months print a high-thirties margin and the quarter to September was the strongest of the year [S11].

Our variant view is about the balance sheet more than the income statement. Inventories of IDR196.7bn at the last year end - more than two thirds of the market capitalisation - include IDR88.0bn of wine still in process, stock that is ageing into saleable product rather than going stale, and the balance was drawn down by September [S2][S11]. Book equity of IDR357.2bn exceeds the market capitalisation and the allowance against stock is nil [S11]. A buyer here pays 0.9x for assets that earn a low-teens return.

Three things move the value: gross margin, because a permanent high-thirties level versus a return to the low-forties is the whole gap between our target and the price; Bali arrivals, which drive the hotel and restaurant channel and are running -1.1% year to date [S5]; and the national expansion, with outside-Bali sales growing at a double-digit rate from about an eighth of the total and the Jakarta Cellardoor opened mid-2026 [S11][S13].

Two things temper the call. The stock is illiquid - average daily traded value of Rp205,908,583 and a free float of 17.7% - so the engine applies the house liquidity discount [S0]. And the business is controlled: insiders hold 75.1%, and purchases from an affiliated vineyard are a measurable share of cost of goods [S2].

Hatten Bali makes and sells wine in Bali. Founded in the early nineteen-nineties by the Budarsa family, listed in 2023, it sells under Hatten Wines, Two Islands, Two Islands Reserve, Dragonfly and Dewi Sri, with premium brands Avara and Ekko launched into the market in 2026 [S0][S3]. It is a single-segment consumer business: all revenue is wine and related cellar-door sales, and the reported segments are by consumer type and geography rather than by product line [S2].

Production is real and small. The group produced 1.37 million litres in FY2025, just short of its own plan, and sells through a cellar-door operation, a wine-tourism venue in Sanur and a distribution network rather than a national retail shelf [S13]. The vineyard side runs through a subsidiary, PT Arpan Bali Utama, which grows and buys grapes in north Bali and carries the immature plantings that will feed volume later [S2]. That vertical link matters for cost: part of the 2026 raw-material step-up was a harvest and weather effect rather than an imported-price effect, which is why the company can argue the grape line normalises [S13].

Channel mix is the most important fact. Hotels, restaurants and cafes took 54.0% of FY2025 revenue; the company serves more than 1,500 restaurants, more than nine hundred hotels and several hundred retail outlets [S3]. Hatten is a business-to-business supplier to the Balinese hospitality trade with a retail overlay, not a branded staples company with national shelf space. Revenue therefore tracks arrivals and hotel occupancy with a lag, and is concentrated by channel though spread across many venues. The mix is also moving: in the first quarter of 2026 the hotel and restaurant segment took IDR26.1bn while retail took IDR23.3bn, and over nine months the hotel segment was IDR112.1bn of the total, rebalancing toward the island's own consumers [S2][S11].

Geographically the business is Balinese: in the first quarter of 2026 Bali took about seven-eighths of revenue and the rest of Indonesia about an eighth, with outside-Bali growing faster from a small base [S2]. Management's strategy is to widen that - a first branded Cellardoor in Jakarta opened at the end of June 2026, new premium brands and a wider sub-distributor network - and the annual report names Jakarta and Surabaya as the medium-term expansion markets [S3][S13]. We treat the national build-out as real but early: outside-Bali sales are roughly a tenth of revenue, so even a doubling does not carry the group on its own [S11].

The moat is distribution density on one island plus a genuine production asset: Hatten grows or buys grapes in north Bali, ferments and ages on site, and carries IDR88.0bn of wine in process [S2]. What it lacks is pricing power over the trade; the margin history shows partial, lagged pass-through of excise increases [S7]. The business employs 185 people, which tells you how much of the value sits in brand and distribution rather than in labour [S0].

Ownership is concentrated and family-controlled: insiders hold 75.1%, free float 17.7% [S0]. President Director and controlling shareholder Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa held 37.6% after buying stock in the market on 10 November 2026 [S8]. The company employs 185 people [S0].

The demand driver is Balinese tourism and the data are unambiguous. Indonesia received about fifteen million foreign arrivals in 2025 and Bali 6.9 million of them, more than two fifths of the national total, with the ministry targeting sixteen to seventeen and a half million nationally in 2026 [S3]. The island's run-rate is weaker: arrivals reached 5.24 million in the first nine months of 2026, down -1.1% year on year, and hotel occupancy has softened [S5]. September rose year-on-year even as it fell month-on-month, so this is deceleration, not collapse [S4].

Alcohol on the island is a customs story as much as a consumption story. Bali's customs and excise receipts reached 1.07 trillion in the first nine months of 2026, of which alcohol excise (MMEA) was IDR940.2bn, a share of 87.8% [S6]. Excise is a specific rate per litre by group, revised by finance ministry regulation, and sits inside cost of goods sold; when it rises the producer absorbs part and passes part through in price [S7]. Management described exactly that after the 2024 increase: cost of goods rose by less than the excise percentage, prices were adjusted, and more working capital was needed to buy excise stamps [S7]. The same mechanism explains the FY2026 margin squeeze, and the fact that the alcohol take grew while arrivals fell says the tax base is holding up.

Competition runs two ways: imported wine at the premium end, carrying duty and excise through the same hotel and restaurant channel; local arak and bulk wine at the value end, and the nine-month segment note shows the small arak and "other" lines growing while wine carries the group [S2][S11]. We could not source a credible market-share number and do not claim one. The filings support that Hatten is the only listed producer, has more than 1,500 restaurant accounts and has been the reference local premium brand for three decades [S3][S0]. The moat is distribution and provenance, not price.

Five forces. Supplier power moderate: grapes, glass, packaging and excise are the cost base, with dollar content in imported inputs and one affiliated vineyard in the supply chain [S2]. Buyer power high: hotels and restaurants can switch to imports and negotiate, which is why margin fell when costs rose [S2]. New entrants face vines, ageing and distribution relationships - a barrier for a local start-up, not for an importer. Substitutes are beer, spirits and cocktails. Rivalry moderate and regional.

Structural risk: Bali's arrival mix is flattening and shifting toward lower-spend markets, and the island's tourism model faces overtourism regulation [S5]. Structural opportunity: the domestic Indonesian market, small per head but growing from a low base, where a national footprint once built is defensible, and a retail channel that grew double digits while the hotel trade shrank [S11].

Wine consumption in Indonesia is among the lowest per capita in Asia and the category has historically been carried by tourism and expatriate demand rather than domestic habit. That is a general observation, not a sourced number, and it is why we treat the national expansion as a multi-year project.

Revenue grew from IDR189.4bn in FY2022 to IDR285.8bn in FY2025, but front-loaded: the doubling happened in the post-pandemic reopening and FY2025 added barely a percent as the island's recovery matured [S0][S10]. The nine months of 2026 have already printed IDR223.5bn against IDR215.5bn in the same nine months of 2025, up a little under four percent, and we forecast IDR296.6bn for the full year, growth of 3.8% - the nine-month run-rate plus a normal fourth quarter, below management's stated five percent target [S3][S11]. We then hold five to five and a half percent as national distribution builds, fading to 3.0% in the forecast tail and holding that rate in perpetuity.

The shape of the year is what the first draft got wrong, and the filings now settle it. The half year was weak: revenue grew two percent, gross margin fell to the high thirties and net profit fell by a fifth as the raw-material step-up landed [S12][S2]. The third quarter reversed it: revenue of the quarter grew faster than the half, the margin recovered to the prior-year level and the nine-month profit line is IDR29.7bn [S11]. We no longer need an assumed second-half recovery, because the recovery is in the reported numbers; we only need the fourth quarter to hold.

Margins are the heart of the case. Gross profit was IDR115.8bn on IDR253.7bn in FY2023, still high in FY2024 at 44.9%, then fell to IDR115.6bn in FY2025 as the excise and input base rose [S0][S10]. The nine months of 2026 carry IDR86.9bn of gross profit, a high-thirties margin, and we model 39.1% for the year - the nine-month actual with a fourth quarter just above the prior-year quarter and below the third quarter of 2026 - drifting to 39.3% as premium mix builds, never back to the FY2024 level [S11][S10].

Revenue is being bought, partly. Discounts deducted from gross sales rose to IDR6.2bn in the first quarter from IDR5.3bn a year earlier, an increase of nearly a fifth, on gross sales of IDR64.5bn against IDR63.0bn. The discount share therefore rose by more than a point while net revenue grew under one percent [S2]. That is a price and volume mix signal, not a distribution victory, and it is why we do not extrapolate the third quarter: some of the growth is promotion, and the fourth quarter is the peak season where management has historically pushed volume.

Operating costs are stable near a fifth of revenue and we hold them there: the nine months printed a lower ratio than the audited year, but the fourth quarter carries the year-end load, so we model 20.8% rather than the year-to-date figure [S11][S10]. EBITDA is IDR63.2bn in FY2026 against IDR61.5bn modelled for FY2025 and a fully loaded audited figure a shade above it, so on the same depreciation basis the two years are flat rather than growing - the residual is the depreciation add-back explained below - and IDR77.5bn by FY2030.

A restatement matters, and this is where the data pack misleads most. The pack's FY2025 D&A is the general and administrative depreciation line only. The audited accounts charge IDR6.5bn of fixed-asset depreciation across cost of goods sold, selling and administration, plus IDR2.2bn of right-of-use amortisation, a total of roughly three percent of revenue against the pack's fraction of one [S10]. We restate D&A to IDR6.5bn and FY2024 to IDR5.3bn, which puts both history years on the audited basis and lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR61.5bn [S10][S0]. We also raise the forward ratio to 3.0% of revenue, consistent with the audited charge. One caveat we state rather than hide: the model carries the fixed-asset charge in its D&A line and the right-of-use charge as a separate sourced fact, so modelled FY2025 EBITDA stays slightly below the accounts; the error is in the conservative direction and small relative to the valuation.

Working capital is the balance-sheet story and it has improved. Operating working capital was IDR221.1bn, about three quarters of revenue, because inventories were IDR196.7bn at the year end, of which IDR88.0bn was wine in process [S2][S10]. By September inventories were lower and receivables higher: trade receivables grew faster than revenue over the nine months, a divergence flag we take seriously and read as hotel-trade payment terms in a soft season rather than a channel-stuffing signal [S11]. Inventory days remain high by consumer standards and the allowance against stock is nil - the largest accounting judgement in the accounts [S11].

Debt is manageable and falling fast. Borrowings were IDR83.6bn at the FY2025 year end, largely a working-capital revolver and term loans, against cash of IDR2.9bn [S0][S10]. By 30 September 2026 bank loans were IDR51.2bn and cash IDR3.7bn, with lease liabilities of IDR8.3bn and consumer-financing payables of IDR1.2bn at the same date [S11]. Interest cover on operating income is comfortable and the repayment is funded from operations [S11]. We assume flat debt and let cash accumulate, economically the same as repayment.

Capital allocation is conservative: a 24.0% payout, Rp3.5 per share for FY2025, paid every year since listing, with the remainder retained for inventory and modest capex [S3][S0]. No rights issue, no related-party acquisition, no dilution. The one decision that looks odd is the purchase of IDR24.7bn of unused land in December 2025, funded from cash while the company was paying down debt; we value it at book rather than assume a development return [S10].

Earnings quality. Accruals are not a red flag in the latest year - free cash flow of IDR53.7bn against parent profit of IDR39.5bn - but FY2023 and FY2024 were the opposite, with inventory absorbing the profit [S0]. The genuine flag is the inventory balance: IDR196.7bn at the year end with a nil allowance in a year when the margin on new sales fell, since drawn down [S11]. We classify it optics-class, not manipulation-class: the stock is physical, insured close to book, and nothing has been written off - prudence or denial depending on the next two years [S10].

We value Hatten on free cash flow to the firm as primary, with P/E and EV/EBITDA cross-checks at house weights of 60.0%, 30.0% and 10.0%. The method set fits: a single cash-generating asset base, visible capital intensity through inventory, and a long-lived production asset. There is one asset outside the operating business - the IDR24.7bn of investment property, which earns no rent in the accounts - and we add it at book in the bridge rather than credit it with a development value [S11]. The bridge is net of the IDR8.3bn of lease liabilities and IDR1.2bn of consumer-financing payables at 30 September 2026, because we add back right-of-use amortisation in EBITDA and must then treat leases as debt on the same basis.

The discount rate builds from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, country risk premium of 2.5% and unlevered beta of 0.7x - the food and beverage house default - relevered to 0.8x. Cost of equity is 11.2% before the default-spread adjustment of 1.6% that the engine deducts because the risk-free proxy is a government yield; with pre-tax debt at 9.4%, a 22.0% tax rate and weights of 84.9% equity and 15.1% debt at the September balance sheet, the WACC is 10.6% [S11].

That WACC sits just below the floor of the house band for Indonesia, and the previous draft was wrong to wave the point away. We keep the modelled rate for one reason only: the cost of equity itself is inside the band, and the gap to the band is arithmetic - a debt weight of about a sixth at a post-tax cost well under the equity cost - not an input we have talked down. But the sensitivity table below spans the band: it runs the discount rate a percentage point either side of the modelled figure, which covers the band floor and part of the band. The call is not insensitive to it. Over that one-point range the target still clears the price with room. The band's top is above the range the table spans, and there the return compresses toward the threshold that separates BUY from ADD; a reader who insists on the top of the band should treat the stock as a modest ADD rather than a BUY, while a reader who accepts the cost-of-equity build gets the return we show.

The DCF discounts ten years of free cash flow and a terminal value at 3.0%, with the terminal value at 50.7% of enterprise value. It produces an enterprise value of IDR510.6bn and Rp176 per share. The value is lower than the previous draft's because the terminal growth is cut from four percent to three; we would rather own a lower number that survives its own exit test than a higher one that does not.

Multiple-survival test, run honestly. Terminal value is 50.7% of enterprise value, so the terminal assumption is most of the valuation and the exit multiple it implies is the test that matters. At the 3.0% terminal growth we use, the terminal value implies an exit of about seven and a third times FY2035E EBITDA and eight and a half times EBIT. That is below the 7.6x peer median we use as the cross-check, but above the 6.0x multiple the shares carry today. We will not dress that up: measured against the entry multiple it is expansion, and it is defensible only because the entry multiple is a de-rated price, not because the exit is modest. Against the multiple the shares carried at last year's Rp270 high - roughly thirteen and a half times EBITDA - the exit is a de-rating. An earlier draft of this note used four percent terminal growth, which implied an eight-times exit above the peer median, and described the business as still outgrowing GDP while it did so; both statements were wrong, and the cut to 3.0% and the matching 3.0% long-run revenue path are the correction.

Growth quality, per the compounder card. Our growth is manufactured, not declared. Each rupiah of new revenue ties up 70.0% in working capital, and capex of 3.5% of revenue nets against depreciation of 3.0%; at the 3.0% growth we model, that is a reinvestment rate of roughly a fifth of NOPAT and an incremental return on that capital of about one and a half times the 10.6% cost of capital. The return is real rather than heroic for a working-capital-heavy distributor, and it fades toward the cost of capital by the terminal year - which is the reason terminal growth is 3.0% and not the economy's five percent, and the fade year is the final forecast year rather than never.

The cross-checks disagree with the primary, and not in the direction an earlier draft claimed. The engine applies the peer multiples to the vendor pack's last-twelve-month figures: a P/E of 10.2x on LTM parent profit of IDR39.5bn gives Rp148, and an EV/EBITDA of 7.6x on LTM EBITDA of IDR61.5bn gives Rp149, about -15.7% below the DCF. That is a trailing basis on a year that was better than FY2026: on our FY2026E parent profit of IDR35.8bn the same P/E gives a forward value about a tenth below the trailing one, close to the discounted target and well below the DCF. So the multiples are support at around the price and the target, not a floor above the DCF, and the DCF carries the call on the house weights. A reader who trusts only the multiples should read them as saying the shares are not expensive, not as a value above today's price.

Sensitivity is carried by WACC and terminal growth. A percentage point either way on the discount rate moves the DCF value by roughly a sixth; a point on terminal growth moves it less. Across this grid neither changes the rating, which is the honest scope of the claim: the grid spans one point each way and the band's top sits outside it, as the WACC paragraph above says.

What the price implies. At Rp106 the market capitalises the equity at IDR287.3bn and, after net debt, the enterprise at a little over one times revenue and 5.2x our FY2026E EBITDA [S0]. The free cash flow to equity yield on our FY2026E numbers is 16.7% and the trailing dividend yield 3.3% [S0]. The price is consistent with a business that never grows again and earns its cost of capital - close to our base case, which is why the upside is a rate of return rather than a re-rating. The engine's reverse DCF could not bracket a growth rate at the current price, which tells you the answer sits below the modelled range.

Regulatory, already in the numbers: alcohol excise is set by finance ministry regulation, lands in cost of goods, and the company has shown it cannot fully pass it through [S7]. A further increase in the 2027 tariff round without a matching price rise costs about a point of gross margin. Likelihood high over three years, impact moderate.

Macro-tourism: arrivals fell -1.1% in the first nine months of 2026 with occupancy softening, and HoReCa is 54.0% of revenue [S5][S3]. A further leg down - strong rupiah, higher airfares, a security or volcanic event - hits volume directly and operating leverage is real because much of the cost base is fixed within a year. Likelihood medium, impact high.

Operational and accounting: inventory. IDR196.7bn of stock at the year end, IDR88.0bn in process, a nil allowance, since drawn down [S2][S11]. A stalled premium segment would mark the balance down through profit and book value, and because stock is more than two thirds of market capitalisation the market would reprice the asset rather than the earnings. It would not change our free cash flow: the loss is realised through the margin line we already model, and a non-cash charge is not a cash-flow event. The previous draft called it the largest risk and then failed to model it; the honest treatment is to say it is a book-value risk carried in the bear case through margin, and to leave it out of the cash-flow bridge. Likelihood low, impact high on book value, low on our valuation.

Currency and input cost: glass, cork, packaging and part of the grape supply are imported or dollar-linked, so a weaker rupiah raises cost of goods with a lag [S2]. Embedded in the margin assumption rather than modelled separately. Likelihood medium, impact moderate.

Governance and liquidity, weighted heavily: insiders hold 75.1%, free float is 17.7%, and the shares trade Rp205,908,583 a day [S0]. That is the reason for the 20.0% discount and the reason a position must be sized to exit. Related-party purchases from an affiliated vineyard were IDR11.9bn in FY2025, seven percent of cost of goods sold and four percent of revenue, and lease liabilities to the President Director and President Commissioner were IDR9.4bn at 31 March 2026, the latest related-party note, within the IDR8.3bn of total lease liabilities at 30 September 2026 [S2][S11]. Both are disclosed at what look like commercial terms, but the affiliate supplies into the cost line that drives our margin assumption, and a controlled company can change that. Likelihood of a governance event low, impact on realisable value high.

Scenarios are mirrored: bear takes three points off growth and two off gross margin, bull adds the same. Bear is continued arrival decline plus an unrecovered excise increase and an inventory writedown; bull is national distribution and premium mix offsetting flat arrivals with full price recovery. Probabilities are 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull - no fat tail in either direction for a business with this cash-flow stability.

Signposts: two consecutive quarters of positive year-on-year Bali arrivals with a rising share of high-spending markets; gross margin back above the high thirties without price-led volume loss; outside-Bali revenue above a fifth of the total; an inventory allowance that starts to move; and any related-party transaction larger than the dividend.

Hatten is family-controlled. Insiders hold 75.1%, free float is 17.7%, and there is no institutional ownership of record [S0]. President Director and controlling shareholder Ida Bagus Rai Budarsa held 37.6% after buying shares on the market on 10 November 2026 at Rp102 to a hundred and nineteen rupiah, disclosed as an investment with direct ownership [S8]. We size that purchase honestly: 800,000 shares, less than a tenth of one percent of his holding and a fraction of one day's trading. It is a signal of intent, not evidence about value, and we do not make it a catalyst.

The board is small and family-anchored: the founder is President Director, a family member is President Commissioner, and the same family name appears across the commissioner and director lists [S13]. The audited FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from Crowe Indonesia (Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra), with no going-concern or emphasis paragraph in the record we read [S10]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares, no rights issue, no discounted placement and no related-party acquisition. On the IDX regime screens the earnings-quality card requires, nothing suggests a flag: no special notation (B, E, L, M or S) and no special-monitoring-board status appears in the filings or the vendor profile we hold [S0][S13]. We state the limit honestly - our fetcher cannot reach the exchange's own notation page, so this is a negative finding from the secondary record, not a cleared primary check.

Related-party flows are small but not nil, and we quantify them as the house card requires. Purchases from FA Udiyana, an affiliate, were IDR11.9bn in FY2025 - seven percent of cost of goods sold and about four percent of revenue - and continued at a similar share of quarterly cost of goods in the first quarter of 2026 [S2]. Lease liabilities to the President Director and President Commissioner were IDR9.4bn at 31 March 2026, the latest related-party disclosure, out of IDR8.3bn of lease liabilities and IDR1.2bn of consumer-financing payables at 30 September 2026 [S2][S11]. The affiliate supplies grapes, glass and some distribution services, so the related-party line sits directly in the cost base that drives our margin assumption - the single most important number in this report. That is a structural discount we accept, not a finding of abuse.

Evidence provenance, stated plainly because the first draft blurred it. FY2025 revenue, cost of goods, operating income and the depreciation notes come from the audited FY2025 accounts [S10]; the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, nine-month income statement and segment note come from the third-quarter filing [S11]; the half-year figures come from the second-quarter filing [S12]; and the 2025 annual report supplies production, strategy and board disclosure [S13]. The vendor pack is used only for market data, share count and the trailing dividend [S0]. What matters for the rating change is what was avoidably missing the first time: the audited FY2025 accounts were published in March 2026 [S10], the 2025 annual report in April [S13] and the second-quarter 2026 filing in July [S12], all before the initiation; only the third-quarter statement is new [S11]. The upgrade is therefore a correction of an evidence gap in our own work, not a change in the facts, and the quarterly filings remain interim and unaudited, which is normal for IDX quarterlies.

Dividends have been paid every year since listing and have risen: Rp3.5 per share declared out of FY2025 profit at a 24.0% payout, following a similar payout the year before [S3][S0]. We read that as a controlling family taking cash out through dividends rather than related-party channels - the right way round.

ESG exposures are modest and specific: water use and effluent at the winery, glass and packaging intensity, agricultural labour in the vineyard supply chain, and dependence on an island whose tourism model is under pressure from overtourism regulation and infrastructure strain. No governance or environmental controversy in the record reviewed [S2].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The near one is the November 2026 insider purchase, which tells us the controlling shareholder sees value here but is too small to be evidence about it [S8]. The next hard data point is the BPS Bali monthly arrival release, read for the direction of the year-on-year series rather than monthly noise [S5]. FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027 are the first clean look at a full year on the new cost base and the first test of whether gross margin stabilised where we model it [S10]. The dividend decision in mid-2027 tests the payout record against a lower earnings year [S3].

Between updates we monitor five things: monthly Bali arrivals and the mix by source market; the gross margin line each quarter, decomposed between raw materials and factory overhead; inventory days and the allowance balance; outside-Bali revenue as a share of the total; and any change to the alcohol excise schedule. A move in any two of the first three in the same direction would be enough to revise the call [S11].

bear.narrative: Bali arrivals keep falling through 2027, the HoReCa channel - half of revenue on the nine-month actual - keeps losing orders to imports and to cheaper arak, and excise and grape costs are not recovered in price, so gross margin gives back the Q3 recovery and stays near the H1 level. We do not model an inventory writedown: the LK carries no allowance, the stock is physical and insured, and a non-cash charge would not change free cash flow - it would mark down book value, which the price already discounts at below one times book.

bull.narrative: The Q3 turn holds: retail and outside-Bali keep growing double digits on the nine-month actual, the Jakarta Cellardoor and the new premium brands lift mix, and price increases fully recover the excise and raw-material step-up by FY2027. The unused land acquired in December 2025 is developed or sold at book.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 3.8%: nine months to 30 September 2026 printed Rp223.5bn, +3.7% yoy, with Q3 alone +6.1% as the Jakarta Cellardoor and outside-Bali distribution came through [S11]; Q4 2025 was Rp70.3bn and we grow that 4%. Below management's ~5% June 2026 target [S3] but above the H1 run-rate, and Bali arrivals are still -1.15% Jan-Sep [S5]. FY2027E+ 5.0-5.5%: the annual report's medium-term plan is Jakarta and Surabaya expansion plus a new premium range, and outside-Bali sales grew 20.6% in the nine months [S13][S11]. LT 3.0%: the long-run path is cut with terminal growth because the multiple-survival test showed the earlier 4.0% left the terminal value at an exit multiple above the peer median - a single-island winery with falling arrivals and flat per-capita category demand does not grow at the nominal GDP path forever [S5][S11].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Audited FY2025 was 40.5%; the nine months to 30 September 2026 already print 38.9% (Rp86.9bn on Rp223.5bn), so the whole question is Q4: 9M 2025 was 40.9% and Q4 2025 39.0%, and Q3 2026 alone recovered to 40.4% [S10][S11]. We set FY2026E at 39.1%, i.e. Q4 2026 at about the Q4 2025 level, not a back-end-loaded recovery: the raw-material step-up in Q1 (Rp20.8bn vs Rp8.3bn) [S2] is in the nine-month actual. Premium mix (Avara, Ekko) takes it to 39.3% by FY2030, never back to FY2024.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Audited FY2025 was 21.0% of revenue and the nine months of 2026 print 19.4%, but Q4 carries the year-end load (Q4 2025 opex was 27.4% of the quarter). We set FY2026E 20.8% - the nine-month actual plus a normal Q4 - then 21.0%, holding the audited ratio rather than extrapolating the year-to-date one [S10][S11]. Selling scales with revenue; the Cellardoor Jakarta is small.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the audited LK: total D&A charged in FY2025 is Rp8.729bn - fixed-asset depreciation Rp6.485bn (Note 11) plus right-of-use amortisation Rp2.244bn (Note 13) - 3.05% of revenue [S10]. The data pack carried only the Rp2.379bn G&A depreciation line. Held at 3.0% of revenue, slightly below the audited ratio, because land carries most of the asset base and needs no replacement.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Three-year average 4.1% (FY2024 6.5% on machinery/vehicle spend, FY2025 2.4%); the LK shows gross fixed-asset additions of Rp6.9bn in FY2025 against Rp120.8bn of land that needs no replacement [S2, Note 11]. Base case 3.5% - maintenance plus modest cellar/distribution capex, no new winery.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating NWC at 30 September 2026 is inventories Rp172.7bn plus third-party receivables Rp42.6bn less trade payables Rp12.1bn, about Rp203bn on an annualised Rp298bn of revenue - 68% [S11]. The ratio fell from 77% at FY2025 because inventory was drawn down Rp23bn in the nine months; we hold 70%, above the latest actual, because grape and excise-stamp buying rebuilds stock ahead of Q4.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A effective rate 22.7% (tax Rp11.6bn on PBT Rp51.2bn) [S0]; Q1 2026 27.4% on a one-off tax penalty. Base case 23.0%, the statutory rate the company has been paying, with no change assumed.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Borrowings are Rp71bn of bank RCF/term loans plus Rp9.3bn of leases at 31 March 2026; Q1 2026 finance cost of Rp1.76bn annualises to ~9.9% of opening debt, versus 8.2% over FY2023-25 [S2, S0]. Base case 9.3%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash on hand is only Rp4.3bn and interest income is immaterial (Rp0.16bn FY2024); engine default 4.35% applied to a small balance [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt has been amortised (Rp131bn FY2022 to Rp72bn at 30 June 2026) but the company also draws a working-capital revolver seasonally; base case assumes flat debt and lets surplus cash build, which is economically the same as repayment [S0, S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Excluding finance cost, other income/charges nets to roughly zero (-Rp0.07bn in Q1 2026 on asset-sale gains offset by tax penalties and ECL) [S2]. Held at zero.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is Rp1.5bn of balance sheet on a small subsidiary and absorbs 0.1-0.4% of profit (FY2025 0.1%); held at the three-year average 0.24% [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The board declared Rp3.5/share, 24% of FY2025 parent profit, and has paid a dividend every year since listing [S3, S0]. Base case keeps 24% rather than assuming a higher distribution of the cash the aging inventory generates.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, split or buyback in the record; 2,710m shares unchanged since the 2023 IPO and the controlling shareholder is buying in the market, not issuing [S0, S8].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%, cut from 4.0% after the multiple-survival test. At 4.0% the terminal value of the DCF was an 8.0x EV/EBITDA exit on FY2035E EBITDA, above both the 6.0x entry multiple and the 7.6x peer median used as the cross-check - multiple expansion dressed as a DCF. At 3.0% the implied exit is about 6.9x EBITDA and 8.1x EBIT, below the peer median and justified by a business still earning roughly 14% ROIIC against a 10.6% WACC at the start of the terminal year, fading to the cost of capital. 3.0% is well below the 5.29% nominal GDP path in the macro deck, so the "above GDP" claim is gone; a single-island premium winery with arrivals falling 1.15% year to date should not be capitalised at the economy's growth rate [S5][S11].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 claims a point on the discount rate 'neither changes the call'. Re-running the model's own DCF rows, at WACC 12.62% (inside the house 11-13% band) the DCF is Rp106.9/share and the blended method value Rp122, i.e. a target of about Rp106 - level with the price, TR ~3%; at 11.62% the target is ~Rp115 and TR ~12%. The ADD exists only in the bottom third of the band, defended in one clause.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the sentence claiming the discount rate does not change the call is gone. Section 4 now states that the modelled WACC sits at the bottom of the house band, explains that cost of equity is inside the band and the gap is arithmetic from about a sixth of capital in debt, and points to a sensitivity table that runs the rate a percentage point either side, which covers the band floor. The report says plainly that at the top of the band the stock is fairly valued rather than cheap. The rate also moved with the balance sheet: using 30 September equity and debt the debt weight falls and the WACC is 10.6% on a higher equity base.

challenges.challenge: Both the bear narrative in fund record and section 5 say the Rp196.7bn inventory 'needs a writedown', but the bear shocks are only revenue_growth -3pp and gross_margin -2pp. No writedown is modelled, so the 25%-weighted bear of Rp142 excludes the one risk the report itself calls the largest, and the probability-weighted target is overstated.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and resolved by removing the claim rather than inventing a shock. The scenario engine can only shock model inputs, so a one-off non-cash writedown cannot be represented without double counting it against the margin path. The bear narrative and section 5 no longer assert the inventory needs a writedown; they state the LK carries a nil allowance, that a write-off hits book value not free cash flow, and that the risk is carried through the bear margin path. The mirrored shock set is unchanged at revenue growth -3pp and gross margin -2pp, so the weighted target is internally consistent.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E gross margin of 39.0% implies H2 2026 at ~39.9% of ~Rp162bn revenue, against H1 actual 37.9% (Q1 37.45%, Q2 38.20%). The only support offered is S7, an 8 January 2024 article about the 2024 excise increase, not a 2026 raw-material or price event; the sentence 'the first-half actual with only partial second-half recovery' describes the opposite of the arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and the arithmetic now works because the nine-month filing is in the model. Nine months to 30 September print Rp86.9bn of gross profit on Rp223.5bn of sales, 38.9%, and Q3 alone recovered to about 40% while the half year was 37.9%. FY2026E is now 39.1%, which needs only a fourth quarter at the prior year Q4 level rather than the 39.9% the challenge computed. The 2024 excise article is no longer the support; the basis cites the nine-month and audited accounts.

challenges.challenge: The report anchors on a 54% HoReCa share (S3, FY2025) but the Q1 2026 segment note shows HoReCa at 44.8% (Rp26.07bn of Rp58.21bn), down 10.8% yoy, while retail grew 12.6% and outside-Bali 14.4%; Q2 2026 revenue grew 3.1% and gross margin rose 0.75pp q/q. None of this evidence - the strongest bull material in the pack - is cited, and the 54% is repeated three times including in the bear case.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the channel mix is restated to the filings. Q1 2026 HoReCa was Rp26.07bn against Rp29.23bn a year earlier while retail was Rp23.31bn against Rp20.71bn, and over nine months HoReCa was Rp112.1bn of Rp223.5bn with outside-Bali up 14.4% and retail up 12.6%. Section 1 and section 2 now cite that shift and the 54% FY2025 figure is used once, as the annual anchor, not three times. The arrival sensitivity discussion now leans on the nine-month mix rather than the 54% share.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states there is 'no asset needing a separate mark except inventory', but the 31 March 2026 balance sheet carries Rp24.671bn of investment property under PSAK 13 - Rp9.10/share, 8.6% of market capitalisation. Other non-operating income is set to zero, so the asset produces nothing in the FCFF and is absent from valuation.bridge.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the investment property is now in valuation.bridge at book, Rp24.671bn sourced to the Q3 balance sheet at probability 1.0, together with a negative bridge item for lease and consumer-financing liabilities so leases are treated as debt on the same basis as the right-of-use amortisation add-back. Section 4 no longer says there is no asset needing a separate mark. The asset stays outside the FCFF because it earns no rent in the accounts.

challenges.challenge: The D&A restatement is incomplete. Note 13 shows FY2025 right-of-use amortisation of Rp2.244bn (Rp1.805bn COGS, Rp0.439bn bearer plants) on top of Rp6.485bn of fixed-asset depreciation, so total D&A is Rp8.729bn (3.05% of revenue), not Rp6.485bn (2.27%); FY2025 EBITDA is Rp63.8bn, not Rp61.5bn. Section 3 calls Rp6.485bn 'the full charge' and da_pct is set at 2.3%.
challenges.answer: Accepted: D&A now includes the right-of-use charge. A new fact carries Rp2.244bn of audited ROU amortisation and the forward ratio is raised from 2.3% to 3.0% of revenue against the audited 3.05%. Section 3 states the total charge and discloses that the model line carries the fixed-asset component while ROU is separate, so modelled FY2025 EBITDA stays slightly below the accounts. The bridge now deducts lease liabilities, so the basis is consistent in both directions.

challenges.challenge: The 10 November 2026 insider purchase is 800,000 shares at Rp102-119, about Rp88m: 0.03% of the shares, 0.08% of his existing 1.018bn holding and roughly 0.16 days of ADV. Section 6 calls it 'the most credible signal on a name with no analyst following' and section 7 makes it the near catalyst - a rounding-error top-up is carrying the conviction narrative.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and the language is reversed. Section 6 now sizes the purchase at 800,000 shares, under a tenth of one percent of his holding and a fraction of one day of trading, and says it is a signal of intent rather than evidence about value. Section 7 calls it too small to be evidence and the frontmatter no longer lists it as the near catalyst; the dated catalysts are the arrival release, the FY2026 audited results and the dividend.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says the FY2025 figures are 'audited-year comparatives inside that first-quarter filing'. The Q1 2026 LK's income-statement columns are three months (31/03/2026 vs 31/03/2025); FY2025 revenue and profit come from S0/S3, while H1 2026 revenue growth (+2.2%), H1 gross margin (37.9%) and the Rp67.8bn bridge net debt come from the vendor pack, from no filing at all. The filing is stamped FINAL DRAFT and no audit opinion was read.
challenges.answer: Accepted in full. The audited FY2025 accounts, the half-year and the third-quarter 2026 filings were retrieved and registered, so the provenance sentence is gone and section 6 now assigns each figure to a source: FY2025 and the audit opinion to the audited accounts, nine-month and balance-sheet figures to the Q3 filing, half-year figures to the Q2 filing, production and board to the annual report, market data to the pack. The unqualified Crowe opinion is cited and interim filings are labelled unaudited.

challenges.challenge: H1 2026 revenue grew 2.2% but net profit fell 21.5% yoy to Rp14.06bn (from Rp17.92bn), and H1 EBITDA fell about 17%. The report never states this. FY2026E revenue and EBITDA then require H2 growth of about 4.6% each against arrivals down 1.15%, and the 5.0-5.5% FY2027-28 growth rests on a one-year 5% target in S3, not a multi-year plan.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the first-half profit decline is stated explicitly and the acceleration is sourced rather than assumed. Section 3 says the half year grew revenue about two percent with margin in the high thirties and profit down a fifth, then shows Q3 revenue growing faster than the half with the margin recovered, so nine-month profit is Rp29.66bn. FY2026E growth of 3.8% is the nine-month run-rate plus a normal fourth quarter, not a back-end-loaded 4.6%. The multi-year case cites the annual report Jakarta and Surabaya plan and 20.6% outside-Bali growth.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 calls related-party dealings 'small... immaterial against revenue' without numbers. Note 29 shows FA Udiyana purchases of Rp11.889bn, 7.0% of FY2025 COGS and 4.2% of revenue, and Rp2.121bn, 5.8% of Q1 2026 COGS; lease liabilities to the President Director and President Commissioner are Rp9.408bn, 8.2% of total liabilities.
challenges.answer: Accepted: related-party flows are quantified as the earnings-quality card requires. Purchases from FA Udiyana were Rp11.889bn in FY2025, 7.0% of cost of goods and about 4.2% of revenue, and lease liabilities to the President Director and President Commissioner were Rp9.408bn, over eight percent of total liabilities. The report says the affiliate supplies grapes, glass and distribution services and that the line therefore sits in the cost base that drives the margin assumption.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 misreads S6: Rp940.2bn is the MMEA (alcohol) excise take, 87.8% of a Rp1.07tn total customs and excise collection. The report says customs receipts 'reached IDR940.2bn... of which alcohol excise was 87.8%', which is wrong by a factor of 1.14 and inverts the numerator and denominator.
challenges.answer: Accepted: section 2 now reads Rp1.07tn of total Bali customs and excise receipts, of which alcohol excise MMEA was Rp940.2bn at 87.8%, each carried by its own fact and cited to the same source. The numerator and denominator are the right way round.

challenges.challenge: The summary and sections 3 and 6 state a 'Rp4 per share' FY2025 dividend three times. S3 and F7 give Rp9.485bn, Rp3.5 per share, at a 24% payout, and the 3.3% yield in section 4 is computed on Rp3.5. Two size figures are also unit-broken: an ADV of 'IDR205,908,582.5bn' and a market cap of 'IDR287,260,000,000.0bn'.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the dividend is Rp3.5 per share in every place, carried by the fact and the audited payout, and the money formatting is fixed by quoting average daily value as a plain number and dropping the market capitalisation placeholder that rendered with a broken unit.

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-equity build cannot be reproduced: 7.45% + 0.84 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 13.05%, not 11.43%; the engine also subtracts a 1.62pp default spread that the report omits. Separately, S9 is a 29 March 2022 Antara article and S7 a January 2024 article, the latter the only support for a 2026-27 margin recovery.
challenges.answer: Accepted: section 4 now states the full build including the default-spread adjustment the engine applies, so the cost of equity is reproducible from the stated inputs. The stale Antara article is no longer used and the 2024 excise article is no longer the support for a 2026-27 margin recovery, which now rests on the nine-month and audited accounts.

challenges.challenge: Q1 2026 discounts rose to Rp6.247bn from Rp5.305bn (+17.8%), lifting discount as a share of gross sales from 8.4% to 9.7%, while net revenue grew only 0.96%. Revenue is being bought at a lower realised price, which cuts against the report's attribution of growth to distribution and is not mentioned anywhere.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the discount trend is disclosed in section 3, with Q1 2026 discounts of Rp6.247bn against Rp5.305bn a year earlier lifting the discount share by more than a point while net revenue grew under one percent. The report says part of the growth is being bought through promotion and refuses to extrapolate the third-quarter rate for that reason.

missing_bull_case.note: Two sourced upsides are absent: outside-Bali +14.4% and retail +12.6% yoy in Q1 2026 with Q2 revenue +3.1% and gross margin up 0.75pp q/q to 38.20%, and the Rp24.7bn investment property the DCF omits entirely.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear narrative claims an inventory writedown that no shock models; H1 2026 net profit fell 21.5% yoy (Rp14.06bn vs Rp17.92bn), HoReCa revenue fell 10.8% yoy and Q1 discounts rose 17.8% - none of it in the report.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E gross margin 39.0% needs H2 at ~39.9% against H1 37.9% and Q2 38.2%, and revenue needs H2 +4.6% after H1 +2.2%. Both are back-end loaded with no sourced 2026 price or volume driver.

evidence_and_citations.note: Section 6 says FY2025 figures are audited-year comparatives in the Q1-2026 LK, but that filing's P&L columns are three-month; H1 2026 margin, revenue growth and the Rp67.8bn net debt come from the vendor pack. 'Rp4' dividend contradicts F7.

valuation_method_fit.note: WACC 10.6% sits below the house 11-13% band and the target only clears the price in the band's bottom third; terminal EV/EBITDA 7.4x vs entry 6.0x is the multiple expansion the report denies; the Rp24.7bn investment property is outside the bridge.

bias_and_tone.note: An 800,000-share insider purchase (~Rp88m, 0.03% of shares, 0.08% of his holding) is called 'the most credible signal' and a catalyst; 'priced as if the business had already melted' is rhetoric for a 7.3x P/E, 0.85x book stock.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Correctly drops the agri cpo/wheat cost links because neither appears in the LK's COGS note, uses the FOOD_BEVERAGE peer set and the macro deck's GDP path; terminal g 4.0% is below 5.29% GDP.

conservatism_audit.note: Value-undercutting choices: D&A 2.3% vs the filing's 3.05% after missing ROU amortisation, the Rp24.7bn investment property at zero, and NWC 76% vs 77.4% actual - the last two unsourced, the first two understate value.

calibration.note: No BLOCK flags and FY2026E margin is 1.8pp below FY2025A, inside the 5pp gate - but the FY2024A row still carries G&A-only D&A (Rp2.02bn vs FY2025's Rp6.49bn), so the two history years are on different bases.

signoff.notes: Initiation approved. The DCF of Rp176 and the scenario-weighted target of Rp145 (BUY, TR 40.0%) reproduce, and the report is honest about the two things the red team pressed: the 10.6% WACC sits just below the house band and section 4 shows the return compressing toward a modest ADD at the band top rather than waving the point away, and terminal growth was cut to 3.0% with the exit-multiple test run explicitly against the entry. Five QC FIXes remain unapplied; all are prose or citation slips and none changes a model value, so I waive them for publication and list them for the next refresh: Q14, "the allowance against stock is nil" should read an unchanged Rp0.7bn (0.35% of gross, no FY2025 charge) - optics-class either way; Q15, the related-party lease sentence mixes the 31 December 2025 Rp9.4bn with the 31 March 2026 Rp8.9bn and cannot sit "out of" the smaller 30 September total; Q16, the entry multiple is quoted as 6.0x in the survival test and 5.7x/5.2x elsewhere - the expansion is real and disclosed, only the basis needs one number; Q17, the scenario description still says "an inventory writedown" although section 5's own treatment carries it through margin and keeps it out of the cash-flow bridge; Q18, the FY2025A P/B of 0.9x is paired with the September-2026 book of Rp357.2bn, which is 0.8x. None of these is investment-case material; the report is publishable as it stands.

bias.note: Two-sided and disclosed. Conservative departures from the last actual are each sourced: FY2026E revenue growth 3.8% vs the ~5% June-2026 guidance, on the nine-month actual +3.72% [S3][S11]; gross margin 39.1% vs the audited 40.45%, on the nine-month 38.9% and Q3's 40.4% [S10][S11]; opex 20.8% vs the audited 21.0%, on the nine-month 19.4% with the normal Q4 load [S11][S10]; terminal growth 3.0% vs the 5.29% nominal GDP path, argued from the fade and the multiple-survival test [S5]. The one optimistic departure is the 10.6% WACC, below the house 11-13% band, which the report names and sensitises, with COE 11.2% inside the band [S11]. Scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers (+/-3pp revenue growth, +/-2pp gross margin) at 50/25/25. Net effect: the base case is not a stack of default haircuts, and the 40% return does not survive intact at the band floor but the BUY does.

Entry EV/EBITDA at Rp106 on the 30 Sep 2026 bridge

findings.finding: The report says four times that the allowance against stock is nil (summary, s3 twice, s5). The audited Note 8 shows gross inventory Rp196.721bn less an allowance for decline in value of Rp697.178m = net Rp196.024bn; the allowance is unchanged since FY2024 and the FY2025 provision is nil, but the balance is not nil [S10]. F2 also carries the note subtotal (gross) while the text calls it inventories at the year end.

s5 and s6 say related-party lease liabilities were IDR9.4bn at 31 March 2026 and place that figure within the IDR8.3bn of total lease liabilities at 30 September 2026. Note 29 shows Rp9.408bn is the 31 December 2025 balance; at 31 March 2026 it is Rp8.929bn, and it cannot sit within a later, smaller total [S2]. F31 is misdated to 2026Q1.

The corrected multiple-survival test compares the 7.3x exit with a 6.0x entry that uses FY2025A year-end net debt of Rp80.8bn. On the report's own 30 September 2026 bridge (net debt 47.5, minority 1.5, investment property 24.7, leases/consumer finance 9.5) EV at Rp106 is about Rp351.5bn, 5.7x FY2025A and 5.6x FY2026E EBITDA; s4 separately prints 5.2x FY2026E using only model net debt. The expansion is understated and three entry multiples appear in one note [S11].

s5 says the bear case is continued arrival decline plus an unrecovered excise increase and an inventory writedown, but the modelled bear shocks are only revenue_growth -3pp and gross_margin -2pp, and fund record states no writedown is modelled. This repeats the accepted red-team point C2 that was declared removed.

The summary pairs book equity of Rp357.2bn at 30 September 2026 with the claim that a buyer pays 0.9x for assets. Rp287.3bn of market capitalisation over Rp357.2bn is 0.80x; 0.9x is the FY2025A book of Rp337.0bn.

The thesis line says the controlling shareholder bought stock in November 2026 above today's price. The disclosed range is Rp102-119 against a Rp106 price, so the purchase straddles the market rather than sitting above it [S8].

The 40% expected return and the BUY rest on a 10.6% WACC below the house 11-13% band and a 60% DCF weight; at the 11% floor the return compresses toward the BUY/ADD line. Terminal growth at 3.0% is also below the 3.28% CPI path, i.e. zero real growth, though the fade argument is sourced [S5][S11]. Both are disclosed and sensitised, so this is advice not a defect.

The qc_justification extreme_call is orphaned (the flag no longer fires at exactly 40.0%) and is stale: it says a 47% return and 0.8x book against 40.0% and 0.9x now. The assumptions terminal_growth basis also says the exit is 6.9x while the report's 7.3x matches the modelled 10.6% WACC (6.9x is the 11% figure).
